findings.title: Google Calendar credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object instead of the parsed tokens
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse() returns the whole zod safeParse result ({ success: true, data: {...} }), not the parsed data. Here it is assigned to `key` and written straight into the DB via prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } }), so after the first token refresh the stored credential key becomes {"success": true, "data": {access_token: ...}}. On the next instantiation the constructor runs googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) (line 75), which throws because access_token/refresh_token are now nested under `data`. Every Google Calendar credential breaks (availability lookups, booking creation, event updates) after its first refresh, forcing users to disconnect and reconnect. This affects all Google Calendar users regardless of whether the new credential-sync feature is enabled. The fix is to store `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (or have the util return the parsed data).

findings.title: prisma is used but never imported, breaking the build
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error (Cannot find name 'prisma') that will fail type-check/build for the app-store package.

findings.title: Freshly refreshed Salesforce access token is saved to the DB but the connection is built with the old, stale token
findings.body: getClient() fetches a new access token from Salesforce and persists it (lines 75-99), but the returned jsforce.Connection is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the old token read from the credential before the refresh, which is the very token that may be expired. The refreshed token (accessTokenParsed.data.access_token) is never used for this connection, so the new code performs an extra token request on every service instantiation without actually authenticating with the fresh token. It should use accessTokenParsed.data.access_token (and instance_url from the parsed response).

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response, but callers expect the parsed token payload shape of their provider
findings.body: When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the unparsed fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT (never calls .json()). Callers, however, consume whatever their own refreshFunction returned: Google does `const token = res?.data; token.access_token` (Response has no .data → TypeError, silently swallowed by the catch so the old token is kept); HubSpot treats the result as a TokenResponseIF (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined → expiryDate NaN, `setAccessToken(undefined)`, and `key: hubspotRefreshToken` writes the Response object into the credential row, which serializes to `{}` and destroys the credential); zoho-bigin and zohocrm read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `.expires_in` on the Response (undefined → TypeError or wrong data). The sync branch makes the refresh flow broken for google-calendar, hubspot, zoho-bigin and zohocrm. The util needs to parse the JSON and normalize it to the shape each consumer expects, or consumers must handle the Response.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with the credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id
findings.body: refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey) passes `credentialId` (the primary key of the Credential row) as the third argument to refreshOAuthTokens, whose parameter is `userId` and which posts it to the external sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The parent platform will therefore look up and return tokens for the wrong user (or fail to find one), and the returned tokens will be stored on this user's credential — mixing up users' third-party credentials. Every other app passes `credential.userId`; this one should too.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema drops every field except access_token, corrupting stored credentials when sync is enabled
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no meaningful toString), so the intended catch-all does not exist — the second key simply overwrites the first. Combined with zod's default behaviour of stripping unknown keys, parsing any token response with this schema keeps only `access_token` and discards expires_in/expires_in-like fields, scope, instance_url, etc. Consequences when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is on: zoom stores `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000 = NaN` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts line 122) so the token can never be considered valid again; salesforce (which always uses this parser when the flag is on, even though it calls Salesforce directly) permanently loses instance_url from the stored key, breaking future connections; office365 keeps a stale expiry. Zod's .catchall()/.passthrough() or an explicit expiry field is needed.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted, bricking credentials
findings.body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the util sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then merge/write this into the DB: zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (VideoApiAdapter.ts line 120) and office365 spreads the parsed data over the stored credentials (CalendarService.ts line 264). The real refresh token is thereby overwritten with a junk literal — both in sync mode (where the endpoint returns no refresh token) and in normal mode whenever a provider omits a rotated refresh token. Any later refresh attempt (e.g. after disabling the sync feature) will fail with invalid_grant and the user must reconnect the app. The placeholder should not be written back to the stored credential.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by directory name, not App.slug, so the webhook 404s for most major apps
findings.body: The lookup `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` assumes the metadata map is keyed by the App table slug, but it is keyed by app-store directory names: `zoomvideo`, `googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar` — while the corresponding App slugs are `zoom`, `google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar` (see e.g. office365video using getAppKeysFromSlug("msteams") and createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" }) in this PR). For those apps the metadata lookup returns undefined and the endpoint responds 404, making credential sync unusable for Google Calendar, Office 365, MS Teams, Zoom and Lark. The mapping from app slug to the metadata key needs to be resolved differently (e.g. match on metadata type/appId).

findings.title: Webhook overwrites an arbitrary credential when a user has several for the same app, and find-then-create is racy
findings.body: Cal.com allows a user to hold multiple credentials for the same appId (e.g. two Google accounts) and teams to hold their own. `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks whichever row happens to come first and overwrites its key with the pushed tokens, potentially replacing account A's tokens with account B's and silently breaking that connection; team credentials are never matched at all. Additionally the find-then-update/create sequence is not atomic and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId), so two concurrent webhook deliveries for a new credential both find nothing and create duplicates. The payload should identify the exact credential (or the endpoint should enforce a uniqueness constraint and use a transaction/upsert).

findings.title: Unhandled validation/decryption errors produce 500s, and the HTTP method is not restricted
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body), JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) (lines 57-59) are called without try/catch — a malformed body, bad ciphertext or a mismatched CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY throws and results in an unhandled 500 (potentially with stack trace) instead of a 400. The handler also accepts any HTTP method since req.method is never checked. Use safeParse and wrap decryption/JSON.parse to return 400 responses, and reject non-POST requests.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with a plain !== string comparison
findings.body: The shared secret is verified with `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, a non-constant-time comparison that is susceptible to timing attacks. For a secret that alone grants the ability to write arbitrary third-party tokens for any user, use crypto.timingSafeEqual (after length checks) instead.

findings.title: Sync-path token refresh stores expiry_date = now and drops refresh_token/email from the credential key
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry (per the contract documented in refreshOAuthTokens.ts), so `responseBody.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` becomes the current time — the token is considered expired on the very next getToken() call, so every MS Teams API call triggers another refresh request to the sync endpoint. Additionally `key: responseBody` replaces the entire stored credential key, discarding refresh_token and email; if sync is later disabled the credential can no longer be refreshed. The refreshed fields should be merged into the existing key and the expiry read from whatever the endpoint actually returns.

findings.title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the token-refresh sync path
findings.body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint can overwrite any user's stored third-party tokens, and the refreshOAuthTokens/parseRefreshTokenResponse utilities sit on the critical path of every calendar/video integration — a broken response shape here corrupts credentials in the DB (several such issues exist in this PR). At minimum, tests should cover: valid/invalid webhook secret, malformed and undecryptable payloads, create vs update behaviour, apps with multiple credentials per user, and both branches (sync enabled/disabled) of the refresh helpers.
